notes.beat: The unreckoned depths of the Father and Son's love: a plan to redeem the witnesses and conclude the case.
notes.oldNote: He had not reckoned with the depths of the Father's and the Son's love — a plan already in place to do two things at once: redeem the witnesses, and conclude the case. Conceived in love, at infinite cost.
notes.newNote:
He never reckoned with this. While one being in the universe was calculating how to win his case, Someone else was already answering the charge — not with an argument, but with a life laid down.

Sorrow filled heaven when it was understood that man was lost, that the whole family of Adam must die. But this was no afterthought, no scramble for a fix after the fall. The plan was already in place, laid in eternity before the ground ever went wrong. Three times the Son withdrew into the light around the Father to plead man's case — and each time the anxious angels waited. When He came back, His face was calm. A way of escape had been made.

And it cost everything. "Think ye," the angel said, "that the Father yielded up His dearly beloved Son without a struggle? No — it was even a struggle with the God of heaven." One plan, doing two things at once: to stand between guilty man and the wrath he had earned — and by that same death, to destroy the one who held the power of death, so heaven and the new earth would never be disturbed again. The witnesses redeemed. The case closed. Conceived in love, settled at infinite cost — before the accuser ever opened his mouth.

notes.beat: God's first words after the fall: the enmity of Genesis 3:15 — grace planted, two seeds, the Seed crushes the serpent's head.
notes.oldNote: The first recorded words of God after the fall are a declaration of war — but not against us. I will put enmity between thee and the woman, between thy seed and her seed. That enmity is not natural to fallen hearts — God put it there. Grace is that enmity. Two seeds, two lines through history, one promise: the serpent bruises a heel; the Seed crushes a head.
notes.newNote:
The very first thing God does after the fall — before He clothes them, before He speaks a single word of comfort — is turn to the serpent and declare war. But listen to where the battle line falls: *I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed.* Not enmity between God and us. Between the serpent and us.

Here's what's staggering. After they sinned, Adam and Eve weren't naturally God's allies anymore — they had crossed over. Left alone, the whole human family would have linked arms with Satan against heaven. There was no hatred of evil left in them to build on. So God reached in and *put* something there that wasn't there before — a holy resistance, a recoil against the very darkness they'd just embraced. That enmity is not our virtue. It is God's gift. It is grace, planted in hostile ground.

And it splits history into two lines — two seeds running down through every generation. The serpent gets a promise too: a strike, a bruised heel. But the woman's Seed gets the last word — He crushes the serpent's head.

(All heaven mourned that day. But this is the moment the rescue began. When Satan heard those words, he knew his grip on the human race had just been broken.)

notes.beat: The arena is fixed: the whole controversy will be decided on this planet, in the human heart.
notes.oldNote: Before the two lines ever begin, notice what God has just done. In pronouncing the enmity, He fixed the arena of the whole conflict. This war would not be fought with armies of angels in the far reaches of heaven — it would be decided here, on this small planet, in the arena of the human heart. God set the bounds: the controversy would center upon the human race. Every soul born would become a battleground and a witness. Heaven and hell both stake their claim on the same ground — you. The question the universe is watching is not merely who is stronger, but whom the human heart will choose.
notes.newNote:
Before the two bloodlines ever begin their long march through history, listen to what God has just done in that garden. The sentence He speaks over the serpent is not only a curse — it is a prophecy, and it fixes the ground of the entire war. This conflict will not be settled by armies of angels in some far corner of heaven. God draws the boundary lines right here: on this one small planet, and closer still, inside the human heart.

And here is the wonder of it. By nature, fallen man felt no quarrel with the enemy at all — the two were in harmony, not at war. Left alone, our whole race would have drifted into a quiet alliance with the very power that ruined us. So God reaches in and puts something there that was never there before. "I will put enmity" — I will plant, inside you, a resistance to evil you could never have grown on your own. That planted enmity is the first mercy, the seed of every soul that would ever turn back toward Him.

The enemy heard it, and he understood exactly what it meant: his grip on the human heart had just been broken open. By some means, man would now be able to resist him. From that moment the heart of every person born becomes the contested ground — and heaven and hell both stake their claim on the same soil. That soil is you. The whole universe leans in to watch, and the question it is asking is not who is stronger. It is whom your heart will choose.

notes.beat: East of Eden, the first child is born into a fallen, bent nature — the two lines begin.
notes.oldNote: Look again at that closed gate — time has passed east of Eden, and now they carry the first child ever born. He inherits the gate closed behind his parents. Once we sinned, our nature changed — bent away from God. And that broken nature was passed down to every child born since. We don't just commit sins; we inherit a nature that sins. And into that bent world, the woman's seed is born — the two lines begin.
notes.newNote:
Look again at that closed gate — it hasn't moved. But time has passed east of Eden now, and Adam and Eve carry something they've never held before: the first child ever born into this world. And he is born on the wrong side of that gate. He inherits it closed.

Here's what changed the day they ate. It wasn't just a rule broken — their nature bent. Adam himself was shown it: from that day the race would carry "strong inclinations" to pull away from God, a degeneracy passing down through every generation after him. So this child doesn't start where his parents started. He starts already leaning. We don't just commit sins — we inherit a nature that sins. That's the wound none of us chose and all of us carry.

And watch what grows out of that one broken home. Two sons — and Scripture says they were unlike from the start. One comes to God confessing he's a sinner, leaning on a promised Redeemer; the other comes proud, resentful of the curse, wanting God on his own terms. Right here, in the first family, the two lines begin — the seed of the woman and the seed of the enemy. The whole long conflict we've been tracing now runs straight through human hearts. But notice the hope hidden in it: into this bent world, the woman's promised Seed has a lineage now. The rescue is already on its way.

notes.beat: Two brothers, two altars: Abel's prescribed lamb accepted, Cain's self-made offering refused.
notes.srChapter: Cain and Abel and Their Offerings (SR ch. 6)
notes.oldNote: The war reached the first family within one generation. Two brothers, two altars. Abel brings the lamb God prescribed — faith in the promised Seed. Cain brings the fruit of his own labour — religion on his own terms. Heaven accepts one — the smoke of Abel's offering rises, and Cain's altar stays cold. Now watch what refused worship does next.
notes.newNote: The war reached the first family within one generation. Two brothers, two altars — built alike, side by side. Abel brings a lamb, exactly as God had shown them: its blood pointing forward, faith resting wholly on the promised Redeemer to come. Cain builds his altar too, brings his sacrifice too — but only the fruit of his own ground, the product of his own hands. Same religion, right up to a point. Beyond that point, everything divides: Abel comes admitting he needs a Saviour; Cain comes offering God a favor, salvation on his own terms, his own merit. Watch heaven answer. Fire flashes down and consumes Abel's lamb — accepted. Cain's altar stays cold; no token, no light, nothing. And Abel had begged him, gently, to come God's way. Cain — the elder — wouldn't be told by his younger brother. Now watch what refused worship does next.

notes.beat: Cain kills Abel over worship — the pattern set: false worship reaches for a stone.
notes.srChapter: Cain and Abel and Their Offerings (SR ch. 6)
notes.oldNote: Watch how fast the poison runs. This is not a stranger killing a stranger — it is the first brothers, and the trigger is worship. 'Cain talked with Abel his brother: and it came to pass, when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother' (Genesis 4:8). The first human being ever to die dies over an offering — killed by a worshipper whose religion was refused, for the crime of being accepted. Mark the pattern; it runs to the end of the Book: false worship never just disagrees with true worship — sooner or later, it reaches for a stone.
notes.newNote:
Watch how fast the poison runs. This is not a stranger killing a stranger — it is the first two brothers on earth, and what sets it off is worship. Both come to God: one brings the lamb God asked for, in faith of the promised Redeemer; the other brings only the fruit of the ground he tilled — his own work, offered with murmuring, refusing the blood. Fire flashes down from heaven and consumes Abel's gift. Cain's is passed by, and from that moment he hates his brother — not for anything Abel did, but for being accepted.

Watch Abel in his last minutes. He doesn't gloat, he pleads. He points Cain back to the mercy of God, reminds him the wrong is in himself, tells him God loves them both — that's why the innocent One was promised, to bear what they deserved. And while Abel is still defending the goodness of God, Cain's rage burns hotter, because reason itself is telling him his brother is right — and he rises up and kills him. The first human being ever to die, dies over an offering, killed by a worshipper for the crime of being righteous. 'Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him' (Genesis 4:8).

Mark the pattern, because it runs to the last page of the Book: these two brothers are the two roads worship takes, all the way to the end. False worship never merely disagrees with true worship — a life of obedience is a standing reproof to it — so sooner or later, it reaches for a stone.
